[h1]A First Impression Review[/h1]

I shouldn't have liked this, but I did. I'm not a horror fan, but the concept was interesting enough to keep me hooked. It reminds me of the movie [i]Smile[/i]. It’s creepy and has some jumpscares that make you feel uncomfortable, but the intrigue of the puzzles actually sold me, despite not being a puzzle guy.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
- [b]Realistic Interface:[/b] Feels exactly like operating a normal Android phone. It's natural and easy to navigate.
- [b]Clever Puzzles:[/b] The difficulty is just right. You have to really think, like hunting through emails to find a mother’s maiden name for a password reset. 
- [b]The Drama:[/b] There is a good chunk of backstory in the messages. Reading through the texts, like the drama with the mom, felt realistic and wild. It adds weight to the mystery. It actually made me care about the missing women. 
- [b]Great Price:[/b] This game is cheap. It's under $10 at full price, and catching it on sale for under $2 is a big W.
- [b]Good Pacing:[/b] The game pushes you in the right direction. If you finish a task, you’ll get an alert letting you know exactly which app or person to investigate next.

[h1]The Not-So-Good[/h1]
- [b]Awkward Acting:[/b] The acting is a little awkward at times. I definitely laughed at a few moments, but it gets the job done and sells the story.

[b]TLDR:[/b] A neat mystery that makes you want to keep playing to see what happens next. If you like unique puzzles and can handle a bit of a creep factor, it’s worth it.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
☐ Skip It
☐ Buy it on Sale
☑️ Worth it at Full Price

review_text_raw:
!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

review_text_raw:
[h2] Simulacra Review: A Promising Start That Loses Its Way [/h2]

Simulacra is an intriguing, story-driven game that draws players in with its early mystery and atmosphere. However, as the game progresses, it begins to lose momentum, culminating in an abrupt and unsatisfying ending. Despite this, the game is still worth experiencing for those who enjoy narrative-focused titles, though it has a few notable shortcomings.

[h3] The Good: [/h3]

1) Compelling Start: From the beginning, Simulacra presents an engaging and mysterious premise that immediately captures the player's attention. The game’s atmosphere and pacing set the stage for an intriguing narrative.

2) Satisfying Puzzle Solving: For those with a keen eye for detail, solving the puzzles is rewarding. The game often challenges players to analyze small clues, and the sense of satisfaction upon uncovering key pieces of the story is one of its standout features.

3) Impactful Choices: The game does well in giving players the feeling that their choices matter. How you respond to certain characters affects their relationships with you, adding a layer of depth and emotional investment to the experience.

[h3] The Bad: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Gameplay: Unfortunately, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive as the game progresses. The entire experience is confined to a phone screen, and while this fits the premise, it can become tiresome over time, as the game rarely deviates from this formula.

2) Lack of Explanation for the Antagonist: The game’s main antagonist remains cryptic, with little explanation given for their motivations or origins. This leaves players with more questions than answers, which can feel frustrating for those who prefer a clear narrative.

3) Abrupt Ending: One of the biggest letdowns is the ending. For a story-based game, the conclusion should feel like a natural payoff, but instead, it feels rushed and unfinished, leaving many of the game’s intriguing threads unresolved. The game’s narrative feels carried more by its strong start than by its finale.

[h3] The Ugly: [/h3]

1) Repetitive Playthroughs: Replaying the game is a tedious process as players must start from scratch. There is no checkpoint system to revisit critical moments or alter the story’s outcome without going through the entire experience again. This makes multiple playthroughs feel like a chore.

2) Frustrating Achievements: Some of the achievements are either too obscure or require an unreasonable amount of time and patience to unlock. This might be off-putting for those who are not inclined to consult a guide or spend excessive hours grinding.

3) Annoying Sound Effects: While the sound design in Simulacra is generally effective, the game occasionally relies on loud, jarring noises in an attempt to startle the player. These moments feel cheap and detract from the otherwise immersive experience, disrupting the atmosphere rather than enhancing it.

[h3] Conclusion: 6/10 [/h3]

Simulacra has a lot to offer in terms of its mystery and narrative, especially for those who enjoy story-driven experiences. However, the lack of a satisfying ending, repetitive gameplay, and the absence of convenience features like a checkpoint system hold it back from being a truly great game. It’s definitely worth checking out if you’re a fan of mystery and story-focused titles, but if you’re sensitive to flashing lights or sudden loud noises, it might be best to approach with caution.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10
